{"id": "84:14/q08", "question": "What does the verb yaḥūr mean and what usage supports it?", "turns_on": "Whether Labīd's poetic use describes a return to ash or becoming ash; the verse itself is explained through return.", "positions": [{"id": "84:14/q08/p1", "position": "It means to return, turn back, or retrace one's steps; the root also describes repeated movement or return to a former state.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Naḥḥās, al-Wāḥidī, al-Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, and Ibn ʿĀshūr give the return sense. Al-Wāḥidī adds maḥār, the destination. Labīd's meteor returns to ashes after shining; Abū ʿUbayda also cites al-Munakhkhal's wa-lā taḥūrī. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Ibn ʿAbbās cite a Bedouin woman's ḥūrī to her daughter. Al-Qurṭubī compares ḥawārī bread restored to whiteness; Bursevī compares the fuller restoring cloth. Al-Rāghib describes back-and-forth movement in a thing or thought; al-Samīn cites water circulating in a pool, perplexity in an affair, the rotating pulley axle, and returning speech. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ distinguishes h-w-r from h-y-r, notes this form occurs only here, and relates dialogue in 18:34, 18:37 and taḥāwur in 58:1, with derivatives for returning speech, an axle, helper, echo, and round eyes. Ibn ʿĀshūr says return to a former place extends metaphorically to a former condition and Quranic restoration (10:23; 86:8). Elmalılı emphasizes decline from improvement."}, {"id": "84:14/q08/p2", "position": "In Labīd's line, yaḥūr may mean 'become' rather than literally 'return'.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn reports grammarians taking the verb like ṣāra, supported by Labīd's image of a bright meteor becoming ash. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ prefers al-Ṭūsī's 'become' for that poem, while distinguishing the Quranic afterlife sense."}]}
{"id": "84:14/q09", "question": "Is yaḥūr Arabic or described as Abyssinian?", "turns_on": "Whether the word is treated as Arabic on poetic and spoken evidence, Abyssinian by transmitted gloss, or a shared form.", "positions": [{"id": "84:14/q09/p1", "position": "It is an Arabic root meaning return, attested in speech and poetry; the languages may share the form.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Qurṭubī, and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ adduce Labīd and the Bedouin woman's ḥūrī. Al-Qurṭubī allows that Arabic and Abyssinian share the derived word. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ distinguishes Arabic h-w-r from h-y-r, and Ibn ʿAbbās's Labīd citation is presented as Arabic evidence."}, {"id": "84:14/q09/p2", "position": "It is also identified as an Abyssinian word or gloss for 'return'.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima, Dāwūd ibn Abī Hind, and one Ibn ʿAbbās report identify the Abyssinian usage; an ʿIkrima example means 'go back to your family.' Al-Qurṭubī allows a shared derivation. Al-Suyūṭī notes the word in Ibn ʿAbbās's answers to Nāfiʿ ibn al-Azraq; his wider survey assembled over a hundred foreign-origin Quranic terms, combining 27 versified by Ibn al-Subkī, 24 added by Ibn Ḥajar, and sixty-odd of his own, including Salsabīl, Ṭā Hā, Sijjīl, and Kāfūr."}]}
{"id": "84:14/q10", "question": "What does the supplication against ḥawr after kawr mean?", "turns_on": "Which sort of reversal the prayer's ḥawr specifies: religious relapse, general decline, or vacillation.", "positions": [{"id": "84:14/q10/p1", "position": "Seeking refuge from returning to disbelief after faith.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī explains the prayer attributed to the Prophet this way; al-Naḥḥās reports the same explanation as one opinion. Al-Ṭabarī states no grading for the report."}, {"id": "84:14/q10/p2", "position": "Seeking refuge from decline after increase or from a good state to a worse one.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās reports the prophetic supplication and this alternative explanation. Ibn ʿAṭiyya explains ḥawr as retracing one's steps. Bursevī says return from a good state; Elmalılı cites the supplication as a reversal from improvement to loss."}, {"id": "84:14/q10/p3", "position": "Seeking refuge from vacillation after firm progress.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn gives this reading of the saying and associates the root with back-and-forth motion."}]}
{"id": "84:14/q11", "question": "Can yaḥūr function grammatically like ṣāra in Labīd's verse?", "turns_on": "The parsing of ramādan in the cited poem.", "positions": [{"id": "84:14/q11/p1", "position": "Yes; it can govern a nominative subject and an accusative predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn reports grammarians using Labīd's line as evidence, with ramādan as predicate."}, {"id": "84:14/q11/p2", "position": "The poetic ramādan can instead be a circumstantial accusative.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn reports the competing parse, which leaves yaḥūr with its return sense."}]}
{"id": "84:14/q12", "question": "How does this verse explain the punishment described around it?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "84:14/q12/p1", "position": "The person's denial of return explains his fate in the blaze and his hard reckoning.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the assertion explains why the person given his book behind his back burns in Hell; inna carries the explanatory force otherwise expressed by a fāʾ. Al-Biqāʿī links complacent pleasure in sins to hard reckoning and a sorrowful return."}]}
{"id": "84:14/q13", "question": "How does the next verse answer his expectation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "84:14/q13/p1", "position": "Balā affirms that he will return, and God's sight or prior knowledge exposes and threatens him.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, al-Baghawī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Ṭabrisī, and Bursevī read balā as correcting the negated belief. Al-Baghawī and al-Ṭabrisī say God watched him from creation; al-Ṭabrisī reports al-Zajjāj saying God knew him before creation and knew his return. Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the response a threat. Al-Zarkashī reports that many readers and linguists prefer stopping at balā in ten such occurrences because it answers the prior statement independently, though some begin there."}]}
{"id": "84:14/q14", "question": "How is disbelief in return connected to pleasure and sin?", "turns_on": "The notes describe both the effect of denying return on conduct and the effect of sin on belief.", "positions": [{"id": "84:14/q14/p1", "position": "Expecting no return or recompense lets a person pursue worldly pleasure, sin, and heedlessness.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says he neither hoped for reward nor feared punishment; al-Ṭabrisī says he violated prohibitions; Qāshānī says blessings veiled their giver and he trusted time; Bursevī explains his joy by denial of resurrection. Al-Biqāʿī says he enjoys wrongdoing without grieving, Study Quran calls the joy worldly heedlessness, and Iṣlāḥī says he expects no share in the Hereafter. Jishumī condemns restricting aspirations to this life as ending in regret."}, {"id": "84:14/q14/p2", "position": "Immersion in sin turns a person away from the afterlife and makes resurrection seem unlikely.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī explicitly states this causal direction while interpreting return to the Lord for accounting and recompense."}]}
{"id": "84:14/q15", "question": "How does this verse fit the sūra and its predecessor?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "84:14/q15/p1", "position": "It belongs to the division of humanity by its return to God and continues the prior sūra's contrast of reward and punishment.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says 84:7–15 details the return announced in 84:6: believers receive records in their right hands, polytheists behind their backs. Al-Biqāʿī says al-Inshiqāq continues al-Muṭaffifīn's ending, where allies receive reward and enemies punishment after denying resurrection and judgment (83:1)."}]}
{"id": "84:14/q16", "question": "Why does the verse end with yaḥūr rather than yaḥūrā?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "84:14/q16/p1", "position": "The longer ending would change the meaning; the verse keeps the meaningful form despite the surrounding sound pattern.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī says Quranic endings put meaning first while allowing matching sounds where suitable. He cites departures from recurring rhyme in 20:78 and 21:66, then identifies 84:14 as a case where yaḥūrā would alter meaning."}]}
{"id": "84:14/q17", "question": "How were the seven reading schools chosen, and do they exhaust transmitted readings?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "84:14/q17/p1", "position": "They are a later practical selection of trusted regional readers, while other valid transmitted readings remain.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī relays Makkī: early lists had many readers and regional traditions; around 200 AH named schools prevailed, and Ibn Mujāhid later substituted al-Kisāʾī for Yaʿqūb. Ibn Jubayr had earlier chosen five corresponding to five confirmed ʿUthmānic codices; two alleged further codices to Yemen and Bahrain were unconfirmed. The seven were selected as memorization became harder, using trustworthiness, long practice, and broad transmission. Yaʿqūb, Abū Jaʿfar, Shayba, and others still circulated. Criteria are sound heard transmission, Arabic, and codex agreement; Nāfiʿ and ʿĀṣim have the strongest chains, Abū ʿAmr and al-Kisāʾī the most eloquence. Makkī rejects equating the seven readers with the hadith's seven aḥruf because that would exclude other sound readings."}]}

{"id": "84:14/q19", "question": "What does the abrogation objection concern in discussions of Quranic speech?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "84:14/q19/p1", "position": "It concerns spoken content rather than the act of uttering, since a ruling may be abrogated while its recitation remains.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this as the fifth objection."}]}
{"id": "84:15/q01", "question": "What does balā affirm against the preceding denial of return?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "84:15/q01/p1", "position": "The denier certainly will return to God and be resurrected for judgment and recompense.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ says balā begins the affirmative answer to the thought in 84:14; al-Naḥḥās says the person sinned boldly because he thought he would not be raised. Al-Jishumī reports a contrast between the human's belief and God's decisive reply, a return to the afterlife, and a return to the Lord who has always seen him. Al-Baghawī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Qāshānī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī, and Study Quran likewise explain the rebuttal as actual return; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it a threat, and Ibn Kathīr says God recreates him as He first created him and repays good and evil. Al-Biqāʿī adds that he returns humbled, diminished, and ruined; Elmalılı describes death and resurrection as reversal and links the return to 84:6. Al-Wāḥidī attributes the return and resurrection explanation to Muqātil and al-Farrāʾ. Ibn ʿĀshūr says God's message through the Messenger establishes the resurrection denied by the person."}]}
{"id": "84:15/q02", "question": "How does balā function grammatically here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "84:15/q02/p1", "position": "It answers the preceding negation as an independent affirmative response; the following clause begins a new sentence.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn says it answers the negation expressed by lan. Ibn ʿĀshūr says it cancels a negative assertion, may follow a declarative denial as well as a negative question, cites 7:172 and 64:7, and says answer particles begin new sentences. Al-Qurṭubī reports a parsing in which balā affirms the return and the statement of God's sight starts separately. Al-Farrāʾ places the affirmative answer before that statement."}]}
{"id": "84:15/q03", "question": "What is the force of inna in this reply?", "turns_on": "The notes give a rhetorical account of emphasis and a grammatical account of an implied oath; neither disputes the other.", "positions": [{"id": "84:15/q03/p1", "position": "It reinforces the rebuttal of the denier's disbelief in resurrection.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the resurrection was taught by the Messenger and contrasts God's knowledge of the person's state with the person's ignorance, citing 2:216."}, {"id": "84:15/q03/p2", "position": "It introduces the answer to an implicit oath.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn identifies an unspoken oath whose answer begins with inna."}]}
{"id": "84:15/q04", "question": "Why is God called his Lord here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "84:15/q04/p1", "position": "He created and governs the person, knows his deeds, and will hold him accountable.", "reasons": "Muqātil identifies the Lord as the person's creator and witness to his deeds. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reasons from divine lordship and governance to knowledge of acts and their assigned recompense, alongside the human obligation to return. Al-Biqāʿī invokes God's wisdom, justice, and sovereignty; Iṣlāḥī adds divine power and mercy."}]}
{"id": "84:15/q05", "question": "Who is meant by the pronoun in bihi?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "84:15/q05/p1", "position": "The person who thought he would never return.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr specifies that God knows this person's circumstances, not merely his essence."}]}
{"id": "84:15/q06", "question": "Why is bihi placed before basiran?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "84:15/q06/p1", "position": "Its early placement stresses God's sure knowledge of him and suits the verse endings.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr gives both emphasis and the rhyme of the verse endings as reasons."}]}
{"id": "84:15/q07", "question": "What grammatical work does the preposition in bihi do?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "84:15/q07/p1", "position": "It connects basiran to its object and conveys attachment or contact.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the intransitive verb baṣira can mean seeing someone clearly and takes the preposition bāʾ for this connection."}]}
{"id": "84:15/q08", "question": "What does God's being basiran of him encompass?", "turns_on": "The reported explanations specify different objects and temporal ranges for God's sight: deeds and circumstances, lifelong observation, prior knowledge of return, decreed fate, or the time of resurrection.", "positions": [{"id": "84:15/q08/p1", "position": "Complete awareness of his deeds, states, and moral worth for recompense.", "reasons": "Muqātil calls God witness to the person's deeds; al-Naḥḥās says He knows the deeds and destination. Al-Jishumī reports knowledge of the person's states and appropriate recompense and himself says God knows and repays deeds. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says nothing is hidden from God's sight. Al-Qāshānī, Abū Ḥayyān, Ibn Kathīr, al-Biqāʿī, Bursevī, Elmalılı, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī, and Iṣlāḥī relate divine observation to repayment. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls sight a metaphor for complete knowledge, including differing moral worth and the person's circumstances rather than merely his essence."}, {"id": "84:15/q08/p2", "position": "He watched the person continuously from creation until resurrection.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī attributes this temporal span to al-Kalbī. Al-Baghawī says God watched him from creation onward. Al-Qurṭubī reports it as another parsing of the clause. Study Quran also reports observation of all actions over this span."}, {"id": "84:15/q08/p3", "position": "He knew the person even before creating him and knew he would return to Him.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj states both prior knowledge and the eventual return. Al-Wāḥidī reports Abū Isḥāq's same explanation. Al-Qurṭubī gives it as his own explanation."}, {"id": "84:15/q08/p4", "position": "He knows the person's decreed fate, including wretchedness or felicity.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī transmits ʿAṭāʾ's specification of the Preserved Record and its decree of wretchedness and disgrace. Al-Qurṭubī reports a broader alternative of wretchedness or felicity."}, {"id": "84:15/q08/p5", "position": "He knows when He will resurrect the person.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī reports this explanation from Muqātil."}]}
{"id": "84:15/q09", "question": "How does God's sight support return and recompense?", "turns_on": "The notes give both a moral argument from just governance and an argument from God's superior knowledge and revealed statement; they do not expressly set them against one another.", "positions": [{"id": "84:15/q09/p1", "position": "God's knowledge and just governance require resurrection, accounting, and repayment for deeds.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī says an afterlife is required by the obligations imposed on humans. Abū Ḥayyān, al-Qāshānī, and Elmalılı connect observation of deeds with return and requital. Ibn Kathīr specifies good and evil deeds. Al-Biqāʿī says leaving the person unaccountable would contradict wisdom, justice, and sovereignty. Bursevī says divine wisdom requires accounting and warns all accountable people against sin. Ibn ʿĀshūr says differing moral worth requires reward and punishment in eternal life. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī adds God's lordship and charge to humans; Iṣlāḥī cites divine power, wisdom, justice, and mercy and says this argument for Judgment occurs elsewhere."}, {"id": "84:15/q09/p2", "position": "God knows the denier's state and has informed him of resurrection through the Messenger.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the clause explains balā because the Lord had already informed the denier of resurrection; inna strengthens that rebuttal and 2:216 illustrates God's superior knowledge. Al-Jishumī reports the contrast between human disbelief and God's decisive assertion."}]}

{"id": "84:21/q07", "question": "Why is the Qur’an not classified as poetry?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "84:21/q07/p1", "position": "Its opponents did not recognize it as poetry, and incidental meter does not constitute deliberately composed poetry.", "reasons": "Abū Bakr argues that eloquent opponents would have challenged accessible poetry if they had considered the Qur’an poetry; their motive to discredit it also makes it implausible that later readers discovered poetry they missed. Most Arabic specialists require at least two metrical lines, with mismatched meters and rhymes failing the test. Some exclude rajaz, especially a fragment or half-line; others demand four rajaz lines, absent from the Qur’an.
